Article Title: A 66-million-year-old gastropod fossil was found at a 5,000-year-old settlement in Ankara; ancient inhabitants may have brought it there
Article Text:
PC: Anadolu Agency of Turkey

What was the 66-million-year-old fossil found in Ankara

What makes the fossil’s presence at Kulhoyuk rare

Mystery behind the fossil’s presence at Kulhoyuk

How is the fossil connected to the ancient Tethys Sea

How are discoveries helping researchers understand Kulhoyuk

A 66-million-year-old gastropod fossil has been discovered at an archaeological site in Ankara, Turkey. Excavators uncovered the fossil during work at Kulhoyuk in the Oyaca neighbourhood of Ankara’s Golbasi district. Researchers believe it dates to one of the final phases of the Tethys Sea, an ancient body of water that once covered parts of Central Anatolia. The creature existed millions of years before the settlement was established about 5,000 years ago. According to the Anadolu Agency of Turkey, the specimen may have been found elsewhere and later brought to Kulhoyuk by the settlement’s ancient inhabitants.The fossil belongs to a gastropod, a group of mollusks that includes snails and slugs. It was discovered during archaeological excavations at Kulhoyuk, in Ankara’s Golbasi district. Researchers believe the specimen dates to one of the final phases of the Tethys Sea. The ancient sea began forming about 250 million years ago and once covered parts of Central Anatolia. The fossil therefore predates the settlement by millions of years. The discovery connects Kulhoyuk’s archaeological history with a much older geological past and gives researchers another clue about the site’s history.The fossil, however, is about 66 million years old, long before people lived at Kulhoyuk. The gastropod therefore belonged to a much earlier period than the settlement’s inhabitants. Researchers are considering whether ancient residents may have found the fossil elsewhere before bringing it to Kulhoyuk. This would make the discovery different from a fossil found in the geological setting where it originally formed. It also leaves researchers with questions about how the specimen reached the settlement and why its ancient inhabitants may have chosen to keep it there.Researchers are considering whether people living at Kulhoyuk thousands of years ago found the fossil elsewhere and brought it to the settlement. However, this remains a possibility rather than a confirmed explanation for how it got there. Researchers would need to establish where the fossil came from and why ancient inhabitants may have decided to keep it at the site. Its age adds another layer to the mystery, since the people at Kulhoyuk were handling an object that had formed millions of years before their time. The discovery has opened another area of investigation into how the fossil reached the settlement and what significance it may have held for those who lived there.The fossil is believed to date to one of the final phases of the Tethys Sea, an ancient body of water that began forming about 250 million years ago and once covered parts of Central Anatolia. The gastropod lived along the shores of this sea about 66 million years ago before eventually becoming fossilised. Its discovery at Kulhoyuk therefore connects the archaeological site with a much older landscape shaped by the ancient sea. The finding does not indicate that the settlement existed during that period. Instead, it offers a glimpse into the region’s geological past, long before communities were established at Kulhoyuk.The fossil is the latest notable discovery from Kulhoyuk, where archaeological excavations have been underway since 2021. Archaeologists recently found what they described as the earliest-known seed remains of Ankara’s distinctive ‘Sevgi Cicegi’, or Love Flower, inside a 4,000-year-old Hittite vessel. The excavation programme is backed by the Turkish presidency and led by Associate Professor Derya Yilmaz Tekin on behalf of Ankara University and the Culture and Tourism Ministry. The work is continuing to uncover evidence from the site and its long history.
Article Summary: The fossil belongs to a gastropod, a group of mollusks that includes snails and slugs. It was discovered during archaeological excavations at Kulhoyuk, in Ankara’s Golbasi district. Researchers believe the specimen dates to one of the final phases of the Tethys Sea. The ancient sea began forming about 250 million years ago and once covered parts of Central Anatolia.

Article Title: US court blocks Trump administration's four-year visa rule for international students and researchers
Article Text:
US federal court blocks Trump administration's four-year visa rule for international students, researchers, blocking Sept 15 implementation.

Also read:

What the rule sought to change

District court questions DHS's justification

First, it said DHS had failed to conduct a reasoned assessment of the costs and benefits of the new framework. In particular, the agency had not adequately accounted for the potential impact on international student enrolment , research, teaching and the travel of foreign journalists.

, research, teaching and the travel of foreign journalists. Second, DHS had not meaningfully considered less burdensome alternatives to replacing duration of status.

Third, the agency had failed to respond adequately to significant public comments raising concerns about the rule's consequences.

Fourth, it found that DHS had not demonstrated a rational connection between the rule and its stated objectives of protecting national security and preventing fraud and abuse.

Impact on international students and US universities

Concerns over academic freedom and press freedom

Economic and administrative costs

Why the relief applies nationwide

Relief welcomed by international education groups

In a major reprieve for international students, researchers, academics and foreign journalists, a US federal district court has blocked the Trump administration from implementing a new rule that would replace the longstanding ‘duration of status’ system with fixed periods of admission.The district court’s order means that the new framework, which was scheduled to take effect on Sept 15, cannot be implemented for now. The existing duration-of-status framework therefore remains in place nationwide.US District Judge F Dennis Saylor IV of the District of Massachusetts on Monday granted preliminary relief to organisations representing higher education institutions, international educators, journalists and others. The district court postponed the effective date of the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) final rule, while litigation challenging its legality continues.TOI had earlier analysed the new rule.International students were allowed to stay in the US, as long as they were studying. The new rule eliminated this ‘duration of status’ concept and subjected international students (F1 visa holders), exchange visitors (J visa holders) and representatives of foreign media to fixed periods of stay.In a double whammy, the new rule also introduced new restrictions on academic flexibility for international students.The rule was challenged in the district court by the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, the American Federation of Teachers, The NewsGuild-CWA, and others.The ruling is particularly significant for international students pursuing lengthy or evolving academic programmes, including doctoral candidates, as well as researchers and scholars whose work may extend beyond a fixed admission period.Under the duration of status system, international students admitted on F-1 visas may generally remain in the US while pursuing a full course of study and authorised practical training, provided they maintain their immigration status. J-1 exchange visitors, including researchers, professors, teachers and trainees, are similarly admitted for the duration of their approved programme or activity.The system has been in place for decades. The district court noted that duration of status for F visa holders dates back to 1978, while the corresponding system for J visa holders was introduced in 1985.DHS's final rule, published on July 17, sought to replace this arrangement with fixed periods of admission. F-1 and J-1 visa holders would generally be subject to a maximum four-year admission period, regardless of the anticipated length of their educational programme or research.Those requiring additional time would have to apply to US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) for an extension of stay, generally using Form I-539. The rule also provided for a 240-day limit for foreign media representatives holding I visas, subject to an extension process.For students, the proposed change would have had consequences beyond the need to seek extensions. The rule placed restrictions on academic flexibility. Graduate students would generally be prohibited from changing their educational objectives or transferring between institutions, subject to limited exceptions for extenuating circumstances. International students would also generally be required to pursue a subsequent programme at a higher educational level, preventing them from undertaking another programme at the same or a lower level while retaining F-1 status.The rule also reduced the post-completion departure period for F and J visa holders who completed their programmes early to 30 days.Judge Saylor's order found that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in their challenge under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which requires agencies to act reasonably, consider relevant evidence and explain the connection between the facts they identify and the policies they adopt.The district court identified four principal deficiencies in DHS's rulemaking.“The use of such labels does not, however, give DHS license to ignore its statutory obligations,” the judge said, referring to the agency's reliance on national security and border protection.In his order the judge also questioned whether the weak connection between the rule and its stated rationales raised concerns about other, undisclosed objectives, including “greater government control over academic institutions and the press”.The district court stressed that its role was not to decide whether the Trump administration had adopted a wise or unwise policy. Its task was to determine whether DHS had complied with the law when promulgating the regulation.The ruling comes at a time when US universities are heavily dependent on international students, particularly at the graduate level and in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) disciplines.The district court noted that there are approximately 1.6 million individuals in F status and about 500,000 in J status. More than half of all international students major in STEM fields, according to data cited in the order.The judge also highlighted the contribution of international students and scholars to American research, innovation and economic growth. The order referred to evidence that international student alumni had founded 143 of 582 billion-dollar US start-ups, or 25%.The potential impact of the rule was reflected in comments submitted during the rulemaking process. A survey of 1,039 current international students, cited by NAFSA, found that 49% said they would not have enrolled in the US had duration of status been replaced with a fixed admission period. A separate survey of 611 prospective students found that 16% fewer respondents said they were likely to enrol under such a system.The new rule adversely impacted Indian students, as they are the largest contingent of international students. According to the latest Open Doors Report, during the academic year 2024-25, there were 3.6 lakh Indian students in the US constituting nearly 31% of the total number of 11 lakh international students. Experts point out that while the numbers of new students from India is falling, the cohort of Indian students will continue to be significant.The district court also noted that doctoral programmes frequently extend beyond four years. Citing evidence submitted during the rulemaking process, it said the median completion time for doctoral programmes was nearly six years, while bachelor's degrees also often took more than four years. The uncertainty created by the extension process could therefore discourage students from choosing the US, the district court found.The order recorded examples of harm that had allegedly begun even before the rule took effect. Two international students at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and 32 at the University of Maryland, Baltimore, had withdrawn from their programmes, according to evidence cited by the plaintiffs. The University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee had also reported a 42% decline in applications from international students in the academic year in question.The order of district court states that the new system could allow a DHS official, acting on “limited and vague criteria” and without any possibility of appeal, to cut short the academic, research or teaching activities of a non-US citizen. An international student who was only one credit short of graduation, for instance, could be required to leave the US without a degree and without any recourse, the judge said. The resulting uncertainty, it added, would have an obvious deterrent effect on student enrolment.The district court said the requirement to seek extensions from USCIS, where decisions would be discretionary and unappealable, could lead students to choose countries offering more predictable routes to completing their studies.The district court also questioned the effect of the rule on academic flexibility.It observed that international students may legitimately change their research interests, alter their academic objectives, transfer institutions or pursue joint degrees. A fixed system that restricts such changes could disrupt established programmes and impose significant burdens on universities.The order referred to concerns raised by institutions that they were already being forced to reconsider joint and combined degree programmes for international students. It also noted that some students had cancelled international research or conference travel because of uncertainty surrounding the new rule.The proposed 240-day limit for I visa holders raised separate concerns about foreign journalists' ability to develop sources and report effectively in the US. The judge in his order also expressed concern that the system could be abused to punish individuals whose viewpoints or research were disfavoured by officials, or to penalise institutions considered undesirable.DHS had acknowledged that the rule would impose significant compliance costs. Its final analysis projected quantified costs of between $443.1 million and $448.6 million overall, including costs to applicants, universities and other affected parties.The district court, however, found that the agency had not adequately weighed those costs against the asserted benefits.The judge also criticised DHS's response to concerns about a decline in international enrolment. When commenters cited evidence that the new system could deter students, the agency offered no countervailing quantitative study, the order said. Instead, it suggested that universities might fill vacancies left by students who chose not to enrol with other qualified applicants.The district court rejected that as an adequate response to concerns about the loss of highly qualified international graduate students, particularly in fields such as science and technology.It further noted that DHS had not sufficiently explained why existing mechanisms, including the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS), could not be used more effectively to address fraud and national security concerns without replacing duration of status.The plaintiffs had sought relief that would prevent the rule from taking effect. Judge Saylor concluded that the court had authority under Section 705 of the APA to postpone the effective date of the regulation.The judge considered whether relief should be limited to the organisations and institutions represented by the plaintiffs or should apply nationwide.The plaintiffs represented almost 600 public and private institutions, while more than 000 higher-education institutions operate in the US. Limiting relief to the represented parties, the district court said, could require parallel regulatory regimes and repeated, potentially inconsistent determinations about which students and institutions fell within the order’s scope. The situation would be particularly complicated because students regularly transfer institutions or pursue joint degrees. A nationwide order, the judge concluded, would prevent the “chaos and confusion” that a party-specific order would inevitably generate.The district court also held that the final rule directly threatened the benefits provided by international students, researchers and journalists “to the substantial detriment of the American public”. Postponing the rule would not harm the public interest, the judge said, because the measure was not reasonably related to any legitimate DHS objective.The district court therefore postponed the effective date of the final rule in its entirety.However, the order did not finally strike down or vacate the rule. The plaintiffs' requests for vacatur and other final relief were denied without prejudice to being renewed. The underlying litigation will continue.Miriam Feldblum, president and CEO of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, welcomed the decision, saying it recognised the serious and irreparable harm the rule could cause to international students, scholars, higher education institutions and the US economy.“While the case continues, this relief preserves the longstanding system that enables our colleges and universities — and our country — to attract, educate, and retain global talent,” she said.Fanta Aw, executive director and CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, said the nationwide relief was an important step towards preserving a fair and predictable system for international students and scholars.“At a time when countries around the world are competing for talent, the US should be strengthening our ability to attract the best and brightest, not creating new barriers to it,” Fanta Aw said.Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, said the preliminary injunction demonstrated that the administration's proposed limits on the time international scholars had to complete their studies were arbitrary and hostile.The UAW Higher Education Department also welcomed the ruling, saying it was a victory for researchers, graduate workers and postdoctoral fellows who contribute to scientific discoveries and teaching in the US. The department said many of its members were international students and scholars working in fields including medicine, engineering and climate science, and that the stability provided by the duration ofstatus system was essential to their work.The district court's order preserves that system for now, but the legal challenge to DHS's attempt to replace it with fixed periods of admission remains pending.
Article Summary: US federal court blocks Trump administration's four-year visa rule for international students, researchers, blocking Sept 15 implementation. US District Judge F Dennis Saylor IV of the District of Massachusetts granted preliminary relief to organisations representing higher education institutions, international educators, journalists and others.

Article Title: In 1907, New Jersey's Clementon Park opened; after surviving a 1931 fire and a $2.37 million foreclosure rescue in 2021, it has permanently closed; now the 52-acre site goes on sale
Article Text:
The end of a 119-year ride

A rare survivor

After more than a century of welcoming families through its gates, Clementon Park and Splash World in Camden County, New Jersey, has announced the ‘difficult decision’ to close permanently. The landmark amusement park made the announcement on September 9, marking an end to its 119 years of operation. The property is now up for sale.One of New Jersey’s oldest amusement parks, Clementon Park and Splash World, located in Camden County, had operated continuously since 1907, when Theodore Gibbs and his sons opened it as a trolley park. Over the years, it has welcomed millions of visitors, survived the fire in 1931, weathered ownership changes, and, more recently, even navigated the financial turbulence that has claimed many regional parks over the past decade.On September 9, the park said the 2026 season would be its last. The announcement came two days after the park’s final day of operations for the year wrapped up. In a statement, the park authorities said that they were closing permanently and that the park was up for sale. “We are saddened to announce that we have made the difficult decision to close the park and plan to offer the park for sale.”They added, “It has been a privilege to care for a place that has meant so much to generations of families.We are hopeful that we will find a buyer who shares our love for Clementon Park and will carry its history and legacy forward,” the park said in a statement shared on its website. “As we close out our 2026 season, we want to sincerely thank our guests, Season Passholders, team members, and community for being part of another summer at Clementon Park & Splash World. ”They said more details regarding the sale would be shared ‘as they become available’. “Thank you for the memories, the support and five wonderful seasons. We are truly grateful to everyone who has been part of this journey,” they added.IB Parks & Entertainment, the Chicago-based company that has owned the property for five years, didn’t specify any reason for the closure. The company acquired the 52-acre site in 2021 through a foreclosure auction for $2.37 million, just two years after the park had temporarily shut down due to the previous owner’s loan defaults. A brief reopening in June 2021 gave the park another run; however, lower attendance and operating pressures affected the park.Clementon Park & Splash World is one of the oldest operating amusement parks in the world. The park first opened in 1907, when Theodore Gibbs and his two sons introduced it as a traditional ‘trolley park’, built at the end of a transit line. The growing popularity of trolley lines drew visitors from neighbouring Camden. In 1931, a fire nearly destroyed the park, but it survived. The Gibbs family’s original stewardship lasted until 1977, before ownership passed to others. For decades afterwards, the park changed hands repeatedly. In 1993, it underwent a renovation, adding the Splash World waterpark, featuring multiple water slides, a wave pool, a lazy river, and the 13,000-square-foot Aquatic Paradise ‘sprayground’. The renovation cost $5 million, and it also attracted more visitors.Then came the 2019 crisis, when loan defaults left the park dark. The 2021 purchase by IB Parks & Entertainment was a rescue. As the company operates multiple parks across the country, including Indiana Beach and Sahara Sam’s, this rescue gave hope that Clementon might integrate into a larger portfolio.But five years proved insufficient. IB Parks & Entertainment has faced challenges across its holdings. Its New York property, Niagara Amusement Park & Splash World on Grand Island, did not open for the 2026 season, citing attendance and revenue shortfalls.What’s next for the park? The company has offered the property for sale, hoping to find a buyer willing to preserve the park’s legacy. If such a buyer emerges, New Jerseyans may still have a place that holds memories of a century. Whether that’s realistic remains uncertain. Regional parks usually depend on real estate value or development potential as much as operating margins. A 52-acre property in Camden County may appeal more to developers than to potential operators. The future of the park now hangs on its next buyer.
Article Summary: Clementon Park and Splash World in Camden County, New Jersey, has announced the 'difficult decision' to close permanently. The park first opened in 1907, when Theodore Gibbs and his two sons introduced it as a traditional ‘trolley park’ In 1931, a fire nearly destroyed the park, but it survived. In 1993, it underwent a renovation, adding the Splash World waterpark, featuring multiple water slides, a wave pool, a lazy river, and the 13,000-square-foot Aquatic Paradise ‘sprayground’

Article Title: An Ohio community is negotiating to buy 850 acres from a coal company; if successful, the public forest could link about 74,000 acres between Wayne National Forest and Strouds Run State Park
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

From coal-company land to a community forest

A potential 74,000-acre connection

Public recreation and rural traditions

Restoring a landscape shaped by coal mining

An economic opportunity as well as a conservation project

An effort in southeast Ohio could turn roughly 850 acres of former coal-company land into a publicly accessible community forest, creating a major connection between existing protected and recreational lands. Local stakeholders are negotiating with the Sugar Creek Coal and Mining Company to acquire the property in Dover Township and establish the Sugar Creek Community Forest. The project could ultimately link the Bailey’s portion of Wayne National Forest with Strouds Run State Park, connecting about 74,000 acres in Athens County. The details come from the announcement for the upcoming Sugar Creek Community Forest town hall, alongside information published by the Ohio Environmental Council and project partners.The proposed acquisition involves approximately 850 acres in Dover Township that are currently owned by the Sugar Creek Coal and Mining Company. Local stakeholders are working to purchase the land and establish it as the Sugar Creek Community Forest, with the intention that it remains available for community benefit in perpetuity.The proposal is part of a broader effort involving Rising Appalachia and other community, environmental and regional partners.The Ohio Environmental Council describes the project as an attempt to develop a regenerative conservation and economic model in Appalachian Ohio, bringing together nonprofits, foundations, educational institutions, businesses, government officials and local residents. The land has significance beyond its size. It sits in a location where conservation of the property could create a continuous corridor between several existing public and conservation landscapes.One of the most important aspects of the proposal is its potential role as a connector. According to the community announcement, the property is positioned to create a publicly accessible biodiversity, recreation and wildlife corridor linking the Bailey’s portion of the Wayne National Forest with Strouds Run State Park. The resulting connected landscape could encompass about 74,000 acres in Athens County.Earlier, the Ohio Environmental Council described a roughly 900-acre vision that would connect about 75,000 acres of state, federal and private conservation lands. The Trust for Public Land, which is now involved in the project, describes the current effort as protecting more than 845 acres and connecting the community forest to a broader network of trails and public land. The connection could have implications for both people and wildlife. Rather than leaving forests and recreation areas separated by privately held parcels, a community forest could provide a link through which people can move between existing trail and conservation networks while helping maintain habitat connectivity.The proposed forest is intended to be more than a protected tract of woodland. The community announcement says the land could support recreation, biodiversity and wildlife while preserving rural activities such as hunting, foraging and gathering firewood. Similarly, the Trust for Public Land states the project intends to provide residents access to activities including hunting, fishing, foraging and firewood gathering. Its description of the project also includes plans connected to education, sustainable tourism, forest-based businesses and workforce development.That community-use element is central to the idea of a community forest. The Ohio Environmental Council says the Sugar Creek project is grounded in regenerative land management, community input and culturally appropriate economic opportunities. It has also described the initiative as a potential model for community-governed land use in Ohio.The proposal also carries a larger environmental-recovery story. The Sugar Creek property is part of a landscape historically affected by coal mining, and the wider Sunday Creek watershed has faced environmental damage associated with mining. Earlier reporting on the project noted that the Sugar Creek Coal Company ceased mining the property in 1923, while parts of the land have subsequently experienced logging. Rising Appalachia has sought to protect the remaining forest from being divided, logged and developed.Restoration is therefore another major component of the proposed community forest. The project specifically identifies continued ecological restoration of the Sunday Creek Watershed as one of the potential benefits of conserving the property. The project is also connected to work already taking place at Solid Ground Farm, where Rising Appalachia has developed ecological education, workforce training and land-based initiatives. The Ohio Environmental Council says its partnership with Rising Appalachia has included an ecology apprenticeship programme, native fruit and nut plantings and an interpretive trail on former coal-mined land.Supporters see the forest as a potential economic asset for the surrounding community rather than simply a conservation purchase. The community announcement identifies opportunities for local entrepreneurs in land-based food, construction and recreation businesses. The broader project vision also includes sustainable timber and forest products, educational activities and recreation-related enterprises. This approach reflects a larger idea behind the project: that restoring forests and waterways can happen alongside efforts to create livelihoods.For now, however, the proposed forest remains dependent on completing the land acquisition. Local stakeholders are continuing to work towards securing the property and involving residents in decisions about its future. A community town hall is scheduled for September 28 in Chauncey, where residents are being invited to learn more about the proposed Sugar Creek Community Forest and participate in the discussion about what the land could become.
Article Summary: Local stakeholders are negotiating with the Sugar Creek Coal and Mining Company to acquire the property in Dover Township. The project could ultimately link the Bailey’s portion of Wayne National Forest with Strouds Run State Park. The resulting connected landscape could encompass about 74,000 acres in Athens County.

Article Title: Meet Nathan Stafford, the Sydney gardener whose response to a homeless man's request for change went viral: he offered work, then paid him $100
Article Text:
The gardener said the work was his way of allowing Robert to earn the money while also showing him respect.

Stafford explains why he offered work

Robert was also offered food and warm clothes

A homeless man asking for spare change in Sydney received a different kind of help when gardener Nathan Stafford offered him work instead. Stafford was cleaning up a residential street when the man, who introduced himself as Robert, approached him and asked for money because he needed to eat.Robert was pushing his belongings in a trolley while standing in the pouring rain, news.com.au reported. He told Stafford that he lived on the street and that the trolley contained “everything” he owned. Rather than simply handing over money, Stafford asked if Robert would help him clear leaves from the street. “I’m happy to help you out, but would you like to give me a hand?” Stafford replied. “Sure,” Robert said.Stafford then gave him a rake, and the two men worked together to clear the leaves. Once the job was finished, Stafford gave Robert $100. The exchange was recorded and later shared online, where it drew a strong response from viewers.“You helped me out, so I want to help you,” Stafford said as he handed Robert the money. Robert was visibly happy with the payment. “Beautiful, I’m very happy with that. That’ll last me a long time; I’ll have a lot of meals. Thank you brother,” he said.Stafford, who runs Nathan’s Lawns and Gardens, later explained his thinking behind the encounter.He acknowledged that some people might question his decision to ask Robert to work while he was already wet and living on the street.“I had two choices here... some may say I got it wrong,” Stafford wrote while sharing the video online. He said his own experience of homelessness influenced how he responded. Stafford explained that he understood why Robert was asking people for money because he had also done the same when he was living on the street.“As someone that has lived on the street I totally get where this man is coming from,” he wrote. Stafford recalled an incident from his own past when he was homeless. He said he once asked someone for money, but the man refused and instead offered to take him in and buy him dinner. “I actually was so hungry that I was so glad he did. I never forgot that man and those moments in my life many years ago,” Stafford said.That experience shaped the way Stafford approached Robert. He said that while Robert was already soaked by the rain, helping him for a few more minutes would not change the fact that he was wet.The gardener said the work was his way of allowing Robert to earn the money while also showing him respect. “I like to call it giving him some respect in a pretty awful situation and letting him earn that money with some dignity and pride,” Stafford wrote.Stafford also said there was no way he would allow Robert to leave without getting something to eat and receiving fresh, warm clothes.“If you never have lived on the street count yourself lucky as it isn’t a fun place... Also you should know there was no way I was letting him leave without a meal on me around the corner and getting him some fresh new warm clothes,” he wrote.The comments under the video were largely supportive of Stafford's response. Some viewers said that giving Robert a chance to work had helped him feel useful and maintain a sense of dignity.One commenter wrote that Stafford had allowed Robert to “earn the money and feel useful”, adding that this could be something he had not experienced for some time. Another said, “You gave him a sense of purpose, and that’s what’s important.”The video gained attention as Stafford's social media following has grown to 13.3 million across Facebook, Instagram and TikTok. His accounts feature videos of him cleaning gardens and streets for no charge.
Article Summary: Nathan Stafford was cleaning up a residential street when the man approached him and asked for money because he needed to eat. Rather than simply handing over money, Stafford asked if Robert would help him clear leaves from the street. The gardener said the work was his way of allowing Robert to earn the money while also showing him respect. The exchange was recorded and later shared online, where it drew a strong response.

Article Title: Nepal farmers are losing up to 90% of their maize to monkey and wild boars; getting compensation can require 12 documents for a payout capped at Rs 10,000
Article Text:
Image: AP

Nepal farmers’ maize losses reached 90% in Gandaki

Monkeys are the most widely reported crop raiders

Image: AP

Farmers can apply for government relief

Application from the victim or claimant

Photographs of the damaged site or affected person

Damage-assessment or site-verification report, known as a Sarjamin Muchulka

Recommendation from the local ward office

Recommendation from the relevant agriculture or veterinary office

Land registration or land-ownership certificate

Disability or death certificate, where applicable

Health post or hospital recommendation, where applicable

Medical bills, where applicable

Post-mortem report, where applicable

Police report, where applicable

Relationship certificate with a deceased victim, where applicable

Crop-damage relief is capped at Rs 10,000

Land ownership is part of the eligibility rules

Sixteen wildlife species are covered

Crop damage is part of a wider wildlife conflict

Lawmakers seek a national action plan

A government task force is studying the problem

Parliament is examining a national strategy

Nepal has introduced wildlife-risk insurance

The conflict is spreading across agricultural landscapes

Nepal farmers are reporting substantial crop losses from wildlife, with rhesus macaques, wild boars and porcupines among the animals frequently entering agricultural fields. A 2026 study by the National Trust for Nature Conservation found that households surveyed across 44 local government areas lost an average of 50.3% of their maize production to wildlife, while maize losses reached up to 90% in Gandaki Province and 88% in Karnali. The government has a relief mechanism for wildlife-related crop damage, but farmers seeking assistance can be required to submit multiple documents and recommendations. Recent reporting says the process can involve 12 types of documents, while the maximum relief available for damaged grain or standing crops is Rs 10,000 (NPR), subject to the rules and assessment. Lawmakers have now called for a national plan to address rising wildlife-related crop losses.The National Trust for Nature Conservation, with technical support from Tribhuvan University’s Central Department of Zoology, surveyed 1,846 households across 44 local government areas in Nepal’s mid-hill regions for its study of problematic wildlife species.The research examined rhesus macaques, wild boars and porcupines, along with the economic effects of crop damage. It found that maize was the most widely cultivated crop and the most heavily raided among those studied. Households reported an average loss of 312 kg of maize a year, equivalent to 50.3% of their production. The study estimated the economic loss from maize at about Rs 2.5 crore among the surveyed households.The level of damage varied between provinces. The study recorded relative maize losses of up to 90% in Gandaki and 88% in Karnali. Rice losses reached 85% in Sudurpashchim, while wheat losses there reached 90%. The figures represent findings from the surveyed areas and are not a nationwide estimate that 90% of Nepal’s maize crop is being destroyed.Rhesus macaques were the most frequently reported problematic animal in the NTNC survey. Some 98% of respondents identified monkeys as a problem, followed by porcupines at 67% and wild boars at 31%. Researchers also identified barking deer as secondary crop raiders, while leopards were reported as a major cause of livestock losses.Researchers directly counted 20,395 rhesus macaques in the 44 local government areas included in the study. They estimated that at least 104,137 rhesus macaques live across Nepal’s mid-hill region. Some troops recorded during the research contained as many as 198 animals.The wildlife involved also varies by region. The parliamentary motion filed in August said crop damage from monkeys, wild boars and porcupines was particularly severe in Bagmati, Gandaki and Sudurpashchim. Farmers in Koshi have reported damage mainly from monkeys and elephants, while communities in parts of Lumbini and Madhesh have faced damage from monkeys and nilgai, also known as blue bulls.Nepal has a government mechanism for providing relief for damage caused by specified wildlife species. The current relief distribution framework has been in effect since July 2023 and covers 16 wildlife species, including monkeys and blue bulls, alongside species already covered under the earlier provisions.For wildlife-damage claims, farmers may have to provide multiple documents and recommendations. Recent reporting says the process can involve 12 types of documents. The documents and recommendations can include:The documents required depend on the type of wildlife-damage claim. Not all of the documents listed above apply to every case. For crop-damage claims, photographs, damage assessment, local recommendations and land-ownership documents are among the requirements reported by Nepalese outlets.The wildlife-damage relief guidelines provide a maximum of Rs 10,000 for damaged grain, based on an assessment of the loss. For standing crops, the maximum relief is also Rs 10,000, with the payment limited to once per seasonal crop. An individual can receive crop-related relief no more than twice a year.The guidelines provide relief rather than automatic reimbursement of the full value of a crop loss. The amount paid in an individual case depends on the assessment and the conditions specified in the relief framework.The relief guidelines state that authorities can provide relief when wildlife damages crops planted on land with proper ownership documents. Farmers cultivating land without the required ownership documentation can therefore face difficulty qualifying for crop-damage relief.The National Human Rights Commission has examined this issue and recommended changes to allow relief for crops grown on traditionally used, unregistered land in certain circumstances. A parliamentary committee study has similarly highlighted land-title requirements as an issue in the relief system.The current relief framework covers 16 specified wildlife species. They include nilgai, monkeys, elephants, rhinos, tigers, bears, leopards, snow leopards, clouded leopards, wolves, wild dogs or dholes, wild boars, wild buffalo, mugger crocodiles, pythons and gaur.Farmers in Madhesh have also reported crop damage from animals and birds that are outside the specified list. Recent reporting cited deer, peacocks and parrots among species for which local residents have sought inclusion in the relief provisions.Crop destruction is one part of a broader human-wildlife conflict affecting communities across Nepal. Government figures cited in recent reporting recorded 14,821 cases of human-wildlife conflict in Madhesh between mid-July 2024 and mid-July 2025, during which 134 people and 457 animals died.The NTNC study also found that wildlife affected several other crops, including rice, wheat, millet, potato, mustard, oranges and cardamom. Loss proportions for these crops ranged from 18% to 52% across the study areas, although some province-specific losses were considerably higher.The issue reached Nepal’s House of Representatives in August 2026, when lawmakers filed a motion of urgent public importance calling for a comprehensive national action plan to address increasing crop losses caused by wildlife. The motion was proposed by Nepali Congress lawmaker Narendra Kumar Kerung and backed by lawmakers from several political parties.The motion says damage caused by monkeys and wild boars is affecting agricultural production, farmer incomes, food security and rural livelihoods. It calls for a national plan with clear deadlines, adequate funding and defined responsibilities for federal, provincial and local governments.The motion also asks the government to provide Parliament with a consolidated account of previous decisions, studies, spending, programmes and results related to the issue. It proposes that progress on the national action plan be submitted to the relevant parliamentary committee every three months.Nepal’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Environment formed a 15-member technical task force on May 18, 2026 to study human-wildlife conflict. The task force includes representatives of government agencies, conservationists and researchers. Its responsibilities include reviewing previous studies, existing policies, institutional arrangements, relief and compensation systems and earlier management efforts.The task force has been asked to recommend short-, medium- and long-term measures for preventing and managing conflict involving monkeys, wild boars, blue bulls and porcupines.The Agriculture and Natural Resources Committee of Nepal’s Parliament has also been examining a technical report prepared by the task force. The report is titled “A Brief Technical Report on Addressing Human-Wildlife Conflict in Nepal: A National Strategy for Conflict Management, Mitigation and Coexistence.” The committee scheduled a discussion on the report on August 18, 2026.The discussion places the existing relief system alongside broader measures for conflict management and coexistence. The national strategy is being considered as wildlife-related crop damage continues to be reported across multiple provinces.Nepal has also introduced a wildlife-risk insurance policy covering human and property losses caused by wildlife attacks. The Nepal Insurance Authority approved the policy in July 2026, with implementation beginning from July 17.The policy has an annual premium of Rs 1,500 and covers 18 categories of wild animals. According to details reported by the insurance sector, coverage includes up to Rs 1 million for death or permanent disability, Rs 500,000 for temporary total disability, Rs 100,000 for serious-injury treatment and Rs 20,000 for minor-injury treatment.The policy also covers property damage up to Rs 500,000, livestock losses up to Rs 100,000 and agricultural crop damage up to Rs 50,000. The 18 categories covered include elephants, rhinos, tigers, bears, leopards, jackals, deer, wolves, wild dogs, wild boars, crocodiles, Indian bison, pythons, nilgai, monkeys, langurs, blackbuck and orphaned animals.The latest research and government discussions show that wildlife-related crop damage is occurring across several different agricultural regions rather than being concentrated around a single protected area. The NTNC study identified Bagmati, Gandaki and Sudurpashchim as areas where multiple crop-raiding species frequently occur together, while the parliamentary motion highlighted different combinations of wildlife in Koshi, Lumbini and Madhesh.For farmers, the reported losses include staple crops such as maize, rice and wheat as well as commercial crops. Nepal's response is now developing along several tracks, including the existing relief system, a technical review of wildlife-conflict management, parliamentary consideration of a national action plan and the introduction of wildlife-risk insurance.
Article Summary: Nepal farmers are reporting substantial crop losses from wildlife. Rhesus macaques, wild boars and porcupines are among the animals frequently entering agricultural fields. A 2026 study by the National Trust for Nature Conservation found that households surveyed across 44 local government areas lost an average of 50.3% of their maize production to wildlife. Lawmakers have now called for a national plan to address rising wildlife-related crop losses.

Article Title: A UK farmer started with 20 sheep on 18 acres; free grazing beneath solar panels helped her expand to more than 200 sheep and 250 acres
Article Text:
Image AI generated

How solar grazing helped Hannah expand

Benefits for sheep and land

Solar grazing offers farmers new opportunities

Combining farming with renewable energy

For first-generation sheep farmer Hannah Thorogood, gaining access to land beneath solar panels has opened a new chapter in her farming journey. She began with just 20 sheep on 18 acres in Lincolnshire, a scale she says was all she could afford at the time. Today, her flock has grown to more than 200 sheep, while the land available to her has expanded to 250 acres. Free grazing on solar sites has helped the change, where sheep manage grass beneath the panels. Thorogood says the arrangement has given her a “massive leg-up” in an industry where land can be difficult to secure.Solar grazing involves using sheep to manage vegetation growing beneath and around solar panels. Solar farms need grassland to be kept under control, and the Guardian reported that maintaining a typical site can involve tens of acres of grass that would otherwise need mowing or spraying. Those conventional maintenance methods can cost as much as £50,000 a year.Sheep provide an alternative because they can graze in spaces that machinery cannot easily reach. They move between solar panel supports and consume vegetation without heavy mowing equipment.For farmers such as Thorogood, that creates a chance to use land that is already occupied by renewable-energy infrastructure while providing pasture for their animals.Thorogood says the arrangement has brought several benefits for both her flock and the land. She believes the sheep improve soil quality and increase pasture diversity, while their grazing means the land does not need spraying.The panels also provide shelter for the sheep. Thorogood said the land is secure because cameras are present across the site, while technology teams monitor the flock. She added that the solar panels give the animals protection from snow and extreme heat, providing a form of shelter alongside the grazing they offer.As reported by the Guardian, Thorogood's experience comes as farmers across the UK face high costs and limited access to agricultural land. The country has traditionally been largely self-sufficient in sheep meat, but high feed and farming costs, the market and weak profitability have contributed to falling sheep numbers.Nicola Noble of the National Sheep Association described free grazing on solar sites as a “valuable opportunity for new, younger or smaller farmers”. Dr Liz Genever, another Lincolnshire sheep farmer, told the Guardian that free solar grazing had enabled her to triple her sheep numbers and said that reaching the full potential of a nearby solar site could increase her income from sheep from £20,000 to £60,000.The model has been presented as a way of combining renewable-energy generation with agricultural use of the same land. Emilien Simonot of Lightsource BP described suitable solar grazing as a “triple-win” for farming, renewables and society, while Lancaster University professor Alona Armstrong said that this type of multiple land use is vital.Not every solar site is suitable for sheep, and concerns have been raised about biodiversity and whether grazing is always carried out at appropriate stocking densities. Noble also warned that grazing should not simply become a public-relations exercise for solar developers. For Thorogood, though, free access to solar-site pasture has provided something particularly valuable: a way to expand her sheep enterprise when agricultural land would otherwise have been difficult to afford.
Article Summary: Solar grazing involves using sheep to manage vegetation growing beneath and around solar panels. Hannah Thorogood says the arrangement has given her a ‘massive leg-up’ in an industry where land can be difficult to secure. She believes the sheep improve soil quality and increase pasture diversity, while their grazing means the land does not need spraying.

Article Title: Trump rejects calls to slow AI, says US leads China in technology
Article Text: US President Donald Trump on Sunday said the United States is leading China in artificial intelligence and must maintain its edge, declaring that “whoever wins AI wins” as he pushed back against calls for the industry to slow down or face tighter regulation.“We're leading China in AI. We're the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” Trump told reporters when asked if the AI industry should slow down or be more regulated.Trump acknowledged that authorities could introduce safeguards for AI but said concerns being raised about the technology were often exaggerated.“We could put guardrails. We can do this and that. But I think you have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up and they're bringing up things that won't happen,” Trump said.His comments come as the United States and China compete for dominance in AI, with Washington seeking to preserve its technological advantage in a rapidly evolving industry.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump says the U.S. is leading China in artificial intelligence. He pushed back against calls for the industry to slow down or face tighter regulation. His comments come as the United States and China compete for dominance in AI.

Article Title: Japan nuclear operator chief to quit after quake data scandal, reactor restart plans hit
Article Text:
The Hamaoka plant is located in Omaezaki close to the expected route of a major Pacific earthquake.

Data scandal puts restart plans at risk

Japan seeks to revive nuclear power

The president of Chubu Electric Power is set to step down after a scandal involving manipulated earthquake data at its Hamaoka nuclear plant, Japanese media reported on Monday. The company is also expected to abandon plans to restart two reactors at the facility.President Kingo Hayashi and chairman Satoru Katsuno will resign, according to public broadcaster NHK and other local media. Chubu Electric is expected to hold a press conference later on Monday. The company was not immediately available for comment.The Hamaoka plant is in central Japan, near a seismic fault line and an area considered vulnerable to a major earthquake. It has been undergoing regulatory safety checks as Chubu Electric seeks approval to restart two reactors.In January, the operator admitted that it had submitted data to regulators that underestimated the earthquake risks facing the plant. The Nuclear Regulation Authority suspended its safety review process for Hamaoka in late December.A 250-page report by an independent panel, released on Monday, said management pressure contributed to the misconduct. It said the management’s "reprimand" over delays in the restart review had placed pressure on employees and was "one of the factors contributing to the misconduct".The Nikkei business daily reported that Chubu Electric would withdraw its application for the safety review.The estimate of maximum seismic ground motion is a key factor in designing nuclear plants to withstand earthquakes. In September 2023, the NRA approved Chubu Electric’s estimate of 1,200 gal, a unit used to measure ground acceleration during an earthquake.However, the regulator received information from a whistleblower in February last year about possible data fraud.The Hamaoka plant is located in Omaezaki, in Shizuoka prefecture, close to the expected route of a major Pacific earthquake. In 2024, the Japan Meteorological Agency issued its first special advisory over the possibility of a "megaquake" in the Nankai Trough area. The advisory was lifted a week later.Japan largely abandoned nuclear power after the 2011 earthquake and tsunami caused reactors at the Fukushima Daiichi plant to melt down. The country is now seeking to restart nuclear facilities to reduce its dependence on imported fossil fuels, meet rising electricity demand from artificial intelligence and achieve carbon neutrality by 2050.The world’s largest nuclear power plant, Kashiwazaki-Kariwa, resumed operations earlier this year.
Article Summary: President Kingo Hayashi and chairman Satoru Katsuno will resign, according to public broadcaster NHK and other local media. Chubu Electric is expected to hold a press conference later on Monday. The Hamaoka plant is in central Japan, near a seismic fault line and an area considered vulnerable to a major earthquake.

Article Title: Trump faces fresh setback as judge blocks stricter foreign student visa rule
Article Text:
The rule would have ended the decades-old system under which many foreign students could remain in the country for the “duration of status”

Judge warns of wider economic damage

Another setback for President Donald Trump’s administration came on Monday after a federal judge blocked a new rule that would have imposed stricter limits on how long foreign students and journalists can remain in the US.US District Judge F. Dennis Saylor in Boston issued the ruling a day before the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was due to implement the policy. The rule would have ended the decades-old system under which many foreign students could remain in the country for the “duration of status” of their academic programme.Saylor ruled in favour of a coalition of unions and higher education advocacy groups that challenged the policy. He said DHS had adopted the rule based on “exceptionally weak” rationales, rejecting the agency’s arguments that the changes were necessary to combat visa fraud and strengthen national security.Under the rule, F visas for international students and J visas for cultural exchange visitors would have been capped at four years. I visas for foreign journalists, which can currently remain valid for years, would have been limited to 240 days.Students would also have faced tighter restrictions on changing programmes or transferring between universities. The new system would have given them 30 days to leave the US after graduation or after changing to another visa category, down from the previous 60-day grace period.The Trump administration has argued that the changes are needed to prevent people from exploiting the student visa system by repeatedly enrolling in courses to remain in the US.DHS General Counsel James Percival criticised Monday's ruling, saying it would require US Immigration and Customs Enforcement to "permit this rampant abuse of our immigration system.""Come on a student visa, take one class per semester, and stay here for decades," he said.But Saylor, an appointee of Republican President George W. Bush, said the government had failed to properly consider the consequences of replacing a system that had operated for nearly five decades.He said the existing system had enabled tens of millions of foreign students and researchers to study in the US, contributing to "groundbreaking research in science, medicine, and technology, substantial economic growth, and a host of other benefits, often on a vast scale."The judge also warned that major research universities, including Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Harvard, could face hundreds of millions of dollars in costs and declining enrolment."The damage to the higher education system and to the economy of the United States is likely to be catastrophic," Saylor wrote.
Article Summary: US District Judge F. Dennis Saylor in Boston issued the ruling a day before the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was due to implement the policy. The rule would have ended the decades-old system under which many foreign students could remain in the country for the “duration of status” of their academic programme.

Article Title: Russia targeting EU, UK officials? Ukraine’s big claim after drone strike
Article Text:
The drone struck a locomotive at Yahodyn station

A Russian drone strike on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border may have been aimed at a diplomatic train carrying former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson , former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt and European security officials, Ukraine’s state railway operator has claimed.The drone struck a locomotive at Yahodyn station, around 2 km from the Polish border, shortly after the diplomatic train carrying the senior officials had passed through the area. No casualties were reported.According to Ukrzaliznytsia, the diplomatic train had left the station earlier than scheduled after railway authorities adjusted timetables in real time because of the continuing threat of Russian strikes.“It is quite likely that the target of this Russian drone could also have been the diplomatic train,” the railway operator said, according to the Daily Mail.Ukrzaliznytsia later confirmed that the diplomatic train had been at the site shortly before the strike. It said the train was carrying security advisers from several European Union member states, along with former European leaders including Johnson.The delegation had been returning from the Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv.Bildt later shared footage of the attack on X, saying the train struck was not theirs but had been travelling just minutes behind them.“This wasn't our train, but the one just minutes after us by the Polish border crossing,” Bildt said. “It was evacuated as the Russian drone approached and no one was hurt.”Another train carrying former CIA Director David Petraeus was reportedly still at Yahodyn station when the drone struck.Johnson condemned the attack, describing it as “random and senseless” and saying it reflected the kind of attacks Ukrainians face on a daily basis.The incident has raised concerns over the safety of foreign officials travelling through western Ukraine, particularly as the strike occurred close to the border of NATO member Poland.Russia has not said that the diplomatic train was the intended target. Moscow said its forces had targeted infrastructure facilitating the movement of military cargo from Europe into western Ukraine.The strike came amid a broader escalation in long-range attacks. Earlier on Sunday, a Russian drone also hit a truck near the Ukraine-Poland border, temporarily disrupting operations at the Yahodyn-Dorohusk crossing.
Article Summary: The drone struck a locomotive at Yahodyn station, around 2 km from the Polish border, shortly after the diplomatic train carrying senior officials had passed through the area. No casualties were reported. The train was carrying security advisers from several European Union member states, along with former European leaders including Johnson.

Article Title: In 1901, Theodore Roosevelt rushed to Buffalo by train after McKinley died and took office in a friend's library; 125 years later, it is reenacted in the same room
Article Text:
The ceremony took place at about 3:30pm, only hours after McKinley's death

Reenactment on September 14

The 35-word oath repeated

Event livestreamed

On September 14, 1901, Theodore Roosevelt arrived in Buffalo after President William McKinley died from injuries suffered in an assassination attempt. Roosevelt reached the city at 1.30pm and was taken to the home of Ansley Wilcox, a friend who would soon provide the setting for an unexpected presidential inauguration.According to Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site, Roosevelt first went to the home of John Milburn, where McKinley had been staying, to pay his respects to Mrs McKinley. He then returned to the Wilcox home. There, the library was chosen as the place for him to take the oath of office as the 26th president of the United States.The ceremony took place at about 3.30pm, only hours after McKinley's death. A small group was present, including a few newspaper reporters who were allowed to take notes. Photographers were kept out of the room until after the ceremony. Roosevelt also wore formal clothes borrowed from some of the guests who were there.Federal District Judge John R. Hazel administered the oath. Immediately after becoming president, Roosevelt held a short Cabinet meeting in the same library. He then went to the morning room to issue his first presidential proclamation.The room where that ceremony took place is now part of the Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site in Buffalo.On the 125th anniversary of Roosevelt's unexpected inauguration, the site is brought the event back to the same library with a live reenactment.The Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural Site hosted the reenactment on September 14, 2026. The event featured Joe Wiegand, a performer known for portraying Roosevelt.The organisers say the reenactment took place in the very room where Roosevelt took the presidential oath in 1901. Wiegand followed part of the same journey that Roosevelt made more than a century ago. He arrived in Buffalo by train on the afternoon of September 14.According to the event organisers, “TR” was expected to arrive downtown at about 3:45pm, depending on the arrival time of the Amtrak train. He then traveled to the historic Ansley Wilcox House and prepared to take the oath.The reenactment began at 4:30pm. It recreated the moment when Roosevelt formally became president after McKinley's death.The event was presented as an opportunity for visitors to experience the historic ceremony in the place where it happened. The organisers described it as a chance to imagine being “IN the room where it happened”.During the reenactment, Wiegand delivered the 35-word presidential oath that Roosevelt spoke in 1901. He raised his hand and take the oath in the same library.The National Park Service records that Roosevelt had selected the Wilcox library as the most appropriate location for the ceremony. After the oath, he stayed there for a Cabinet meeting before moving to another room to issue his first presidential proclamation.The September 14 reenactment was livestreamed through the Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural Site's social media platforms. However, only a limited number of people were able to watch the event from inside the library.VIP tickets were sold for those who want exclusive access to the live reenactment. The organisers said proceeds will benefit the site's civic education programming.The VIP ticket costed $500 per person or $850 per couple. The ticket also includes access to the site's Exemplary Citizenship Reception scheduled for 6pm on September 15, the following evening. Tickets for the Double-Decker Bus Tour are not included and have to be purchased separately.The Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site is located at 641 Delaware Avenue in Buffalo, New York. The site is operated by the Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural Site Foundation through a cooperative agreement with the National Park Service.
Article Summary: Theodore Roosevelt arrived in Buffalo after President William McKinley died from injuries suffered in an assassination attempt. He was taken to the home of Ansley Wilcox, a friend who would soon provide the setting for an unexpected presidential inauguration. There, the library was chosen as the place for him to take the oath of office as the 26th president of the United States. The room where that ceremony took place is now part of the Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site.

Article Title: Russian businessman funded Trump Jr’s Bahamas wedding after-party
Article Text:
Russian businessman Umar Kremlev

Russian businessman Umar Kremlev, who is reportedly close to President Vladimir Putin, funded the after-party for US President Donald Trump Jr’s wedding in the Bahamas, the Financial Times reported.Trump Jr and his wife Bettina Anderson confirmed Kremlev’s role in an Instagram post, thanking their “dear friend Umar” for hosting “two incredible nights of celebrations”.The couple called it “an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend” and said they were “incredibly grateful”.Kremlev, who heads the International Boxing Association, has reportedly close ties to Putin. He has presented Putin with a diamond boxing glove and later received the Order of Merit to the Fatherland from the Russian president, according to the Financial Times.ProPublica, which first reported Kremlev’s involvement, said he spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the wedding weekend. Kremlev has also been a member of the Russian nationalist biker group Night Wolves.The revelation has raised questions in Washington. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, said: “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the president’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.”Trump Jr and Anderson rejected any political connection, saying: “Friendship doesn’t require a political motive. Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda.” They added “NO CONSPIRACY, NO MYSTERY.”
Article Summary: Umar Kremlev is reportedly close to Russian President Vladimir Putin. He funded the after-party for US President Donald Trump Jr's wedding. Trump Jr and his wife Bettina Anderson confirmed his role in an Instagram post. The couple called it “an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend’

Article Title: A Texas farmer stopped planting cotton and sent his sheep to solar farms; the switch turned a potential $200,000 loss into $300,000 profit
Article Text:
Sheep under solar panels in Lanai, Hawaii. Images Credit: Wikipedia

How did a Texas farmer turn sheep and solar farms into a $300,000 profit

Image Credit: Wikipedia

What made solar farms useful for sheep grazing

How sheep grazing became a profitable farm business

Solar grazing is spreading across American farmland

Importance of this shift for American farmers

Chad Raines, a fourth-generation Texas cotton farmer, stopped planting cotton after years of losses and found a very different way to make a living from his land and livestock. Instead of relying on crops, he began moving sheep between solar farms, where the animals graze on grass growing beneath and around the panels. The change transformed the economics of his farm. According to CBS News, Raines estimated a cotton crop would have cost him nearly $200,000 in losses, while his sheep-grazing operation brought in close to $300,000 in profit.Raines had spent generations in the cotton business, but the numbers were becoming increasingly difficult to justify. According to CBS News, several years of poor harvests and low cotton prices left the family unable to make progress. Debt continued to build, forcing Raines to consider an option far from the traditional row-crop farming his family had followed for four generations.The solution was solar grazing. Raines began providing sheep to solar companies so the animals could feed on vegetation around their panels. Instead of using the flock simply to produce meat, he was being paid for the work the sheep performed on the solar sites.As reported by the Western Producer, Raines did not plant a single cotton seed in the 2024 growing season.He instead rented most of his Texas farmland to a neighbour and spent his time taking his sheep to solar farms. He had agreements with five solar companies, making the grazing work more profitable than growing cotton.Solar farms need vegetation kept under control so grass and other plants do not interfere with their equipment or make maintenance more difficult. Traditionally, this work can involve machinery and workers repeatedly cutting vegetation.Sheep offer a different approach. They can move between rows of panels and feed directly on the grass. One such example of a solar farm is the large Enel North America solar farm near Waco, Texas, with more than one million panels, where sheep are used to manage vegetation. According to CBS, Site manager Adam Sotirakopoulos said that the animals could continue working in conditions when machines might be less practical, including rain, mud and at night.The Western Producer reported that managed grazing can also reduce costs for solar companies. Silicon Ranch, a Tennessee-based solar company, said it saves about 20% in operating expenses on a site with managed grazing. The company noted that paying shepherds can be less expensive than keeping mowing crews and machinery working continuously.Raines did not depend entirely on grazing payments. According to The Western Producer, he also began selling lamb meat to a restaurant supplier. Together, the solar grazing income and lamb sales helped him make about $300,000 in profit. He said the solar payments covered his expenses, including labour and about $2,000 a month spent on food for guard dogs. His son also returned to the farm to help with the growing operation.As reported by CBS News, Raines was grazing about 6,000 sheep across 20,000 acres. The scale gave the family a business that could also provide work for his sons, giving the farm a possible future beyond cotton.The arrangement also changed the nature of the farmer's income. Instead of growing a crop and then accepting whatever price the market offered, grazing contracts gave him a more predictable payment for a service. Other farmers described solar grazing as a way to create steadier income during difficult agricultural years.Raines is part of a much larger shift. The Western Producer reported that sheep grazed on more than 129,000 acres of US solar sites in October 2024, compared with 15,000 acres in 2021. The number of sheep working on solar sites also rose from about 80,000 to more than 113,000 between January and October of that year.According to CyberGuy, sheeps can replace gas-powered mowing crews, reducing maintenance costs and emissions. It also highlighted the Texas operation as an example of how grazing contracts can create another source of income for farmers.For solar companies, the appeal is practical. Sheep naturally eat the vegetation that would otherwise need to be controlled. For farmers, the same animals can generate income without requiring them to plant another crop.The change comes at a difficult time for American agriculture. The Western Producer reported that US cotton futures had fallen nearly 40% over 2 years, while American exports had also declined as cheaper Brazilian supplies and weaker Chinese demand affected the market.Nearly 40% of small and mid-sized US farms operated at a loss in the previous year, according to a 2024 US Department of Agriculture report. For farmers facing high costs and falling returns, finding an additional income source can make the difference between keeping a farm operating and leaving agriculture altogether.For Raines, that choice was particularly stark. Solar grazing gave him another route, turning a difficult farming year into a profitable one while keeping his family involved in agriculture.The result is a unique partnership between livestock and renewable energy. Rows of solar panels provide the setting, while sheep provide the maintenance, and farmers gain an income that traditional cotton farming could no longer reliably provide.
Article Summary: Chad Raines, a fourth-generation Texas cotton farmer, stopped planting cotton after years of losses. Instead of relying on crops, he began moving sheep between solar farms. The animals graze on grass growing beneath and around the panels. Raines estimated a cotton crop would have cost him nearly $200,000 in losses, while his sheep-grazing operation brought in close to $300,000.

Article Title: 'Was laughing': Video shows Indian-origin woman, friend moments before NYC subway train ran over them
Article Text:
An Indian origin woman and her friend were tragically hit by a subway train in NYC.

What happened on the tracks?

Why were they on the tracks?

Who were Malaika Chitre and Navam Kaul?

Indian-origin woman and her friend, both 24-year-old, from New Jersey were fatally struck by a New York City subway train early Sunday after they were seen sitting on the tracks at a Manhattan station. Investigators are trying to determine how and why they ended up in the path of the approaching train.Malaika Chitre and Navam Kaul, both recent Rutgers University graduates, were on the tracks at Spring Street station in Lower Manhattan shortly after 3 am when a southbound No 4 train entered the station. The train operator saw the pair and tried to stop, but was unable to prevent the collision. Both were pronounced dead at the scene. Around 100 passengers were later evacuated from the train, according to reports.The circumstances surrounding the deaths remain unclear. Investigators are examining whether Kaul first fell or went onto the tracks and Chitre followed in an attempt to help him, whether intoxication played a role, or whether the possibility of suicide should be considered.An incident report obtained by the New York Daily News said the train operator told supervisors that she saw the man and woman sitting on the tracks as the train approached.She attempted to stop the train, but it was too late.The report said Chitre appeared to be laughing and pulling Kaul towards her when the train struck them. Separately, law-enforcement sources told the New York Post that Kaul may have fallen or made his way onto the tracks before Chitre went down after him.Video circulating on social media also appeared to show the pair sitting together on the tracks shortly before the train arrived. AmNewYork reported that the operator activated the emergency brake but could not stop the train in time.The medical examiner has not yet released an official determination explaining the circumstances of the deaths.One possibility being examined is that Kaul ended up on the tracks first and Chitre went down to help him.Police sources told the New York Post that it was not immediately clear whether Kaul had fallen or climbed down. Chitre appeared to try to pull him towards her before the train hit them.If that account is confirmed, Chitre may have gone onto the tracks in an attempt to rescue her friend, rather than intentionally placing herself in the path of the train.However, investigators have not established what happened immediately before the pair were seen on the tracks.Investigators are also looking into whether one or both of them were intoxicated and may have been too impaired or disoriented to recognise the danger posed by the approaching train, according to law-enforcement sources.The footage showing the pair apparently remaining on the tracks as the train approached has raised questions about whether they understood what was happening around them. But there has been no official finding that alcohol or drugs were involved, and toxicology results, if any, have not been made public.Suicide has also been posed as a possible explanation.No suicide note was found at the scene, according to sources cited by the New York Post. However, the absence of a note does not by itself establish how the pair came to be on the tracks, and investigators have not concluded that their deaths were intentional.At present, there is no publicly established motive for why the two were on the tracks.Chitre and Kaul were longtime friends who attended Rutgers University around the same time and graduated in 2024.Chitre, from the Dayton section of South Brunswick, New Jersey, graduated from Rutgers with a degree in public health and a minor in business administration. She was working as a quality operations specialist at pharmaceutical company Acadia Pharmaceuticals and had recently begun pursuing a Doctor of Pharmacy degree at Temple University.Kaul, from Sayreville, New Jersey, graduated from Rutgers Business School with a degree in finance. He had been working as a financial data analyst at Bloomberg since 2025.The two were part of the same social circles and South Asian community around Rutgers, according to people who knew them. Rajnikant Pipalia, whose son was a close friend of Kaul, told the New York Post that the pair had grown up in the same social world and remained part of the same wider group of friends.Their deaths came as they were beginning their professional lives.
Article Summary: Malaika Chitre and Navam Kaul, both 24, were on the tracks at Spring Street station in Lower Manhattan when a southbound No 4 train entered the station.
